title: API generation changes and platform renaming

opening.headline: When the API generation changes and platform names and paths change as well, you learn how to read the impact by dividing it into compatibility, functionality, and path.
body: The service continues to work well using the previous API, so the need for migration is not immediately apparent. However, OpenAI is migrating from Chat Completions to the Responses API, Google is moving from its Vertex AI lineup to the Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform, and Anthropic has compiled migration guides detailing code changes specific to each model.

In this class, we sequentially review transition announcements from three companies and verify how document search terms, console menus, permission names, and environment variable values become misaligned when names change. We also practice a method of evaluating the impact of transitions along three axes: compatibility, functionality, and path, using two case studies.
opening.objectivesLead: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:
objectives: Can explain what API generation transition (such as Responses API) and platform name and path changes entail.
The effects of transition can be analyzed by distinguishing them into compatibility, functionality, and path.

screens.title: API generations change, and so do their names and paths.
screens.lead: First, please read about the direction in which the vendors are moving.

visual.alt: A three-arrow sequence indicating the transition from an old name to a new name, together with a list of items misaligned below it.
labels: Together, what is out of alignment

paragraphs: OpenAI is migrating from Chat Completions to the Responses API. The documentation states that Chat Completions will continue to be supported, but recommends using Responses for new projects. Google has renamed its Vertex AI product line to the Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform, and also provides documentation on how to move between the Gemini Developer API and the Gemini Platform API.

When the name changes, the surrounding environment becomes misaligned before the code does. Document search terms change, console menu names and permission names differ, and values specified in environment variables or configuration files no longer match the new approach. Since services continue to operate properly using the previous API, these misalignments do not become apparent until after the transition begins.

In this class, the impact is divided into three aspects: compatibility, which checks whether the existing request operates as before; functionality, which evaluates the benefits provided by the new API; and routing, which examines changes to endpoints, projects, and permissions.

callout.label: Things to think about
callout.text: If the reason for the transition is not simply that the service has stopped, then what should we use as the basis to determine when and in what order to move?

screens.outro: First, let's recall which API our current service is using.

screens.title: Are there any services currently using the previous API?
screens.lead: When you select each question, the instructor's thoughts unfold. You won't have to enter or submit your answer, so think about it in your head first and then press it.

items.prompt: Is there a service currently using the previous API? Which SDK version and endpoint does that service use?
items.answer: To plan a transition, you must know which API generation for each service is called using which SDK. Even for the same provider, services may have different generations. Without this information, you cannot determine the scope of the transition.

items.prompt: Configuration containing platform names, for example, are project, region, and permissions embedded in the code?
items.answer: If names or paths are directly hardcoded throughout the code, changes to the name require modifications in multiple locations. Google clients generate project and location values at creation time, so having these values consolidated in a single place makes them easier to read and manage.

items.prompt: Who is affected when determining the transition timeline?
items.answer: Not only the development team modifying the call code, but also the security team managing permissions, the operations team using dashboards and runbooks, and the support team referencing documentation are affected. This course begins with the observation that a name change spreads beyond the code.

screens.outro: Now I will compare how OpenAI's Chat Completions and Responses differ in the request.

screens.title: OpenAI: Difference between Chat Completions and Responses Requests
screens.lead: Select each tab to compare the call patterns and differences between the two APIs.

visual.alt: A diagram comparing the Messages array and the Items list side by side.

tabs.label: Chat Completions
tabs.body:
Inputs and outputs are **Messages array**. This is a structure that bundles multiple interests into a single object.

``python
completion = client.chat.completions.create(
    model="gpt-6-astra",
    messages=[{"role": "user", "content": "Write a one-sentence bedtime story about a unicorn."}],
)
```

`n` allows receiving multiple responses at once via the `choices` parameter. The documentation states that this API will continue to be supported.

tabs.label: Responses
tabs.body:
Inputs and outputs are composed of **Items**. An Item is a union of multiple types, and thus `message` is an Item, as are `function_call` and `function_call_output`.

In ``python
response = client.responses.create(
    model="gpt-6-astra",
    input="Write a one-sentence bedtime story about a unicorn.",
)
```

`input`, strings or message lists can be provided, and system-level guidance is passed via `instructions`. The response returns only a single generation, with no `n` parameter.

tabs.label: State and Tools
tabs.body:
In Responses, `store: true` can be used to connect inference and tool context across turns. The document explains that Responses stores the object by default, while Chat Completions store the object by default in a new account. To disable storage for both APIs, specify `store: false`.  

Tools are provided natively as web search, file search, computer usage, code interpreter, and remote MCP. The model can call multiple tools within a single API request.

tabs.label: Document recommendations
tabs.body:
The document states that Chat Completions will continue to be supported, but recommends using Responses for new projects. Benefits include improved reasoning performance, an agent loop that works by default, enhanced cache utilization, better state maintenance, and encrypted inference.

Performance and cost improvement figures are from internal OpenAI evaluations. We cannot guarantee that the same improvements have been achieved in our service, so direct measurement is required to verify these results.

screens.outro: The following will check how Google changed its names and access methods.

screens.title: Google: Name change and two Gemini API paths
screens.lead: Examine how the name changes and how the calling convention differs when transitioning between the two states.

states.label: Name change
states.body:
With the introduction of the Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform, the Vertex AI product names have changed. The corresponding table in the documentation has been updated as follows:

- Vertex AI Platform has become Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform.
- Vertex AI Studio has become Agent Studio on Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform.
- Vertex AI Agent Engine has become Agent Runtime on Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform.
- Vertex AI Endpoints has become Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform Endpoints.
- Model names have also changed; "Claude on Vertex AI" now appears as "model name, available on Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform".

These names appear first in document titles, console menus, monitoring labels, and other locations.

states.label: API Path
states.body:
Google provides two API products. The **Gemini Developer API** is the fastest path to build and scale, and is recommended for most developers who do not require specific enterprise controls. The **Gemini Platform API** provides enterprise features based on Google Cloud.

Both services can be accessed using the `google-genai` library (version 2.3.0 or later), with different values when creating a client.

```python
# Gemini Developer API
client = genai.Client()

# Gemini platform API
client = genai.Client(
    enterprise=True, project="your-project-id", location="global"
)
```

Subsequent calls follow the same pattern of passing `model` and `input` to `client.interactions.create`. The documentation introduces the Interactions API as a recommended approach for developing with Gemini models and agents.

screens.outro: Now I'll look at how Anthropic guides model transitions.

screens.title: Read Anthropic's Model Transition Guidance
screens.lead: When an item is selected, the migration guide expands to show what it reveals.

items.prompt: What does the migration guide contain?
items.answer: Anthropic provides a separate migration guide for each model, listing the code changes required when moving from one model to another. The Sonnet 5.5 guide directs users to the appropriate sections based on whether they are coming from Sonnet 5, 4.6, 4.5, or other versions, and organizes the changes into model-specific checklists.

items.prompt: What items cause error 400 when switching to Sonnet 5.5?
items.answer: The guide notifies you of five settings that must be removed from the request. These are: thinking budget, sampling parameters, assistant prefill, forced tool choice, and disabled thinking. If any of these settings remain, the request will fail with a 400 error.

items.prompt: What happens if the thinking field is not specified?
items.answer: In Sonnet 5.5, adaptive reasoning operates by default even without a thinking field. For models version 4.6 and below, the same request was executed without any reasoning. Since responses may begin with a thinking block, code that previously read the response as content[0].text might break, and instead the block must now be read by its type.

items.prompt: Fable 5.1 What does the guide's note on compatibility warnings indicate?
items.answer: Claude Fable 5.1 can read the thinking blocks from previous models, but previous models cannot read the thinking blocks from Fable 5.1. If the system follows a structure where it transitions between models to continue a conversation, its behavior may vary depending on the direction of transition.

items.prompt: How should this change be categorized and interpreted?
items.answer: Broken requests are categorized by compatibility, new behaviors are categorized by functionality, and changes in the target object pointed to by a call—such as a model ID—are categorized by path. These three classifications serve as the basis for the following illustrative examples.

screens.outro: After reading the guidance from the three companies, let's illustrate the impact of the name change on settings and permissions using a practical example.

screens.title: Explanation: Impact of path changes on settings and permissions
screens.lead: The instructor breaks down the scenario where the name has changed step by step. Select the right arrow to proceed to the next step.

steps.title: case
steps.body: The service previously documented and operated under the name Vertex AI is being migrated under the new name Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform. The model and features remain unchanged, but the name and invocation method differ.

steps.title: Find the value that contains the previous name
steps.body: Look for values that contain the previous name in code and settings. Resource names, document links, and monitoring labels are typical examples. Although these values may not appear to affect the call itself, they can cause users to lose their way when searching for documents and dashboards.

steps.title: Verify the project and location.
steps.body: In the new client creation method, `enterprise=True`, `project`, and `location` values must be provided. Verify that the project and location of the existing service match this method. Google documentation advises selecting a region closest to the user but to confirm functionality support.

steps.title: Verify service account permissions
steps.body: Verify that service account permissions and policies are applied to resources in the new path. Even if the functionality is the same, a mismatch between path and permissions may cause the call to fail. If the permission names have changed, the policy documentation must also be updated.

steps.title: Aligns the runbook with the dashboard
steps.body: Update the laptop for emergency contact and the dashboard name to the new designation to prevent technicians from searching using the previous name and finding nothing in case of a failure.

steps.title: result
steps.body: Name changes propagate beyond code to include settings, permissions, documentation, and operational tools. Therefore, compatibility, functionality, and paths must each be individually verified, with the path verification being the key focus in this case.

screens.outro: This time, we'll examine compatibility checks when an API generation changes as a case study.

screens.title: Explanation: Compatibility Check for API Generation Transition
screens.lead: Let's go step by step through an example of migrating a service built with Chat Completions to Responses. Select the right arrow to proceed.

steps.title: case
steps.body: We are moving a customer service chat completion service to Responses. This service features the ability to receive multiple response candidates via the `n` parameter and select one.

steps.title: Compatibility: Finds the broken parts
steps.body: Find the section where the message array should be replaced with Items. Responses can accept strings or message lists via `input`, so simple cases can be easily migrated. However, Responses does not have a `n` parameter and returns only a single response. This service's candidate selection feature must be redesigned using approaches such as sending multiple calls.

steps.title: Function: Inspects code to identify reducible sections
steps.body: Using built-in tools and the `store` option allows you to assess whether you can reduce the amount of custom state management code you need to write. This step must be performed after compatibility checks are complete. Introducing new features first makes it difficult to isolate broken components and distinguish between old and new behaviors.

steps.title: Path: Gather the callout into one place
steps.body: The endpoint and SDK method change from `client.chat.completions.create` to `client.responses.create`. Centralize these calls so you do not have to update many scattered call sites.

steps.title: Performance claims are verified directly.
steps.body: The document states that Responses achieve better performance and cache utilization. However, this is a value derived from OpenAI's internal evaluation metrics. We measure response quality and cost using representative requests from our service.

steps.title: result
steps.body: Migration is not completed in one go. After gathering all call components, conduct category-by-category reviews focusing on compatibility, functionality, and path order, and only introduce what has been verified within the service.

screens.outro: Having examined two cases, I will organize the transition into three axes.

screens.title: The Three Axes of Transition: Compatibility, Functionality, Path
screens.lead: While reading the table, organize and review what each axis represents in terms of questions and check points.

data.caption: Three axes for reading transition impacts
rows: Does the existing request function as intended? Are there any breaking parameters?

Responses lacks the `n` parameter, Sonnet 5.5 throws a 400 error when processing thinking budget and sampling parameters along with assistant prefill, code that previously read the response as content[0].text
Whether to use the tools, state, and inference capabilities provided by the new API
Responses built-in tools and `store: true`, Gemini's Interactions API, and Sonnet 5.5 adaptive thinking
Is the endpoint, project, region, permission, or name changed?

Renaming from `client.chat.completions.create` to `client.responses.create`, `genai.Client(enterprise=True, project, location)`, from Vertex AI to Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform, service account permissions
data.notes: If all three axes are not observed together, a change in one axis can lead to failure in another axis. For example, if you change a path without verifying permissions, the function may behave the same way, but the call will fail. New API features should be introduced only after compatibility checks are completed to ensure safety.

checks.intro: Check for yourself what you just learned. Results are not recorded or graded.
checks.q: Customer service is receiving multiple responses at once via the n parameter of Chat Completions. Based on the documentation, what is the most appropriate judgment?
options: Chat Completions immediately stops operation, so all calls must be migrated immediately.
When moved to Responses, the n parameter operates exactly the same way.
Chat Completions will continue to be supported, so there's no immediate urgency, but when transitioning, the n usage section should be checked for compatibility.
n Parameters can only be used after the model name changes, so first verify the platform name.
checks.explain: The document states that while Chat Completions will continue to be supported, it recommends using Responses for new projects. Since Responses do not have an n parameter, potential issues during transition must be identified in advance.

wrong.0: The document indicates continued support for Chat Completions, stating it will not be discontinued immediately.
wrong.1: n A function that receives multiple responses as parameters is not available in Responses.
wrong.3: n Parameters are unrelated to the model name, and this issue is a compatibility problem.

checks.correctFeedback: Yes. Continued support is available, but compatibility checks are necessary.
checks.incorrectFeedback: Think again. Whether support is provided or not is a separate issue from potential gaps during transition.

This is because the date is missing from the model ID, causing the response structure to be fixed as a simple text entry.
The platform name changed, so the response field name changed from content to another name.
Assistant prefill is automatically enabled because the response prefix is empty.
checks.explain: The guide notes that adaptive thinking operates by default even in the absence of a thinking field. Since responses may begin with a thinking block, code assuming the first item is text will break.

wrong.1: An ID without a date merely refers to a fixed snapshot, regardless of the response structure.
wrong.2: Name change is due to path and configuration issues, and there is no evidence that the response field name has changed.
wrong.3: Assistant prefill is actually a change that causes a 400 error and is not automatically enabled.

checks.correctFeedback: Yes. The response can begin with a fault block.
checks.incorrectFeedback: Think again. Recall the guide and consider where the fundamental operation has changed.

glossary.def: This is an API introduced by OpenAI following Chat Completions. It supports items, instructions, built-in tools, and store options.
Vertex AI products are now grouped under a new name as part of Google Cloud's platform.
This is a change in product and feature names. Documentation, configurations, and labels are affected before the code.
This refers to changes in the path that calls pass through—such as endpoints, projects, regions, or permission policies.
This document summarizes the code changes required when the provider alters the model or API.

misconceptions.myth: Since only the name has changed, the code can remain unchanged.
misconceptions.fact: The name affects settings, permissions, labeling for monitoring, and runbooks. When the name changes, it misaligns document search terms, console menus, and permission names.

misconceptions.myth: This API must be migrated immediately.
misconceptions.fact: If the previous API continues to be supported, simply compare compatibility and benefits to determine the preferred order. However, for new projects, using the new API is recommended as per the documentation.

misconceptions.myth: When switching to a new model, the request code remains unchanged.
misconceptions.fact: The Migration Guide lists items that cause a 400 error due to parameter removal. You should verify the change log in the guide rather than simply changing the model ID.

closing.lead: This summarizes the core content of the class.
points: Transition considers compatibility, functionality, and path together.
Name changes involve more than just settings and permissions.
The features of the new API are introduced after compatibility checks.
Concentrating call flows in one location reduces transition costs.
closing.reflectionLead: The questions below are for your own reflection only and will not be submitted or graded.
closing.reflection: What API generation and platform name does our service use, and which setting will be most affected first if it changes?
